newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ long bond yields close 10 points higher.
newsitem.headline: NZ long bond yields close 10 points higher.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.50 PCT (PREV 9.50) US 30-YR 6.46 (PREV 6.43)
* Long bond yields rise 10 points on light volume
* Bills only rise a couple of points as TWI recovers
* Rumours of further dual currency issue
New Zealand long bond yields drifted 10 points higher by the close on Monday but the short end only weakened slightly as the currency recovered and rumours circulated of another dual currency issue.
The 11/06s got sold to 7.21 percent first thing and drifted higher to finish at 7.25 percent.
"There's just a lack of enthusiasm," said a senior Wellington bond trader. "There's real lack of momentum in the market.

"In quiet periods we are tending to drift up in sentiment instead of consolidating. It looks like we could this week test the higher end of the recent ranges we have seen -- test up to that 7.30-35 percent in the 06s," he said.
There were buyers in the bill market around 9.0 percent and as the Trade-Weighted Index recovered to finish at 67.10. The 7/97 bonds also performed better, only rising around three basis points.
There was a rumour of a dual currency eurokiwi issue and buying, assumed to be related, out of Tokyo.
Weak sentiment in the United States and Australia did not help sentiment in the bond market and New Zealand continued to underperform those markets and the Canadian.
The Statistics New Zealand August employment data due on Tuesday morning will be the critical determinant for direction of the short end of the market.
Dealers did not attribute weakness in the bond market to weekend rumours that New Zealand First was about to finalise a coalition deal with the National Party.
NZ First is in talks with the caretaker National government and the left-of-centre Labour Party about forming a government.

While the wages data -- where economists predict total ordinary time earnings will rise 3.5 percent in the year and private sector ordinary time earnings will be up 4.2 percent -- will be a crucial piece of information for the Reserve Bank, traders believe the bank will want to know who is the government before it eases monetary conditions.
"If the employment numbers are friendly (RB Governor Don) Brash may go earlier than mid-December but I can't see why he would do anything before he knows what the political situation is," said one.
